lines.text: Volcanoes, earthquakes, floods and fires, sinking ships and failing machines. These are the great disasters the world remembers, from the Bronze Age to our own day.
In the Bronze Age, the volcano of Thera in the Aegean blew itself apart, burying the town of Akrotiri and leaving a vast flooded crater.
In the year 79, Vesuvius erupted over the Bay of Naples. Ash and hot gas buried Pompeii and Herculaneum, and froze Roman life in place.
In 1556 an earthquake struck northern China. Homes carved into soft hillsides collapsed, in what may be the deadliest quake ever recorded.
In 1666 a fire began in a London bakery. For days it swept the wooden streets, and most of the old city, St Paul's included, was lost.
On All Saints' Day in 1755, an earthquake, a tsunami and then fire destroyed much of Lisbon, and shook how Europe thought about faith and nature.
In 1783 a long fissure opened in Iceland. Its haze drifted over Europe, the livestock died, and famine followed.
In 1815 Mount Tambora in Indonesia gave the largest eruption in recorded history. It cooled the whole world, and the next year had no summer.
In 1845 blight struck Ireland's potatoes. Hundreds of thousands died of hunger, and more than a million left their homeland.
In 1871 Chicago burned for two days. The wooden city rose again in new ways, and the first skyscrapers followed.
In a winter storm of 1879, the new Tay Bridge in Scotland collapsed beneath a passing train. Engineers learned to reckon with the wind.
In 1883 the island of Krakatoa exploded with one of the loudest sounds ever heard. Its tsunamis killed tens of thousands, and its ash reddened sunsets worldwide.
Four years later the Yellow River burst its banks across the plains of northern China, in one of the deadliest floods on record.
In 1889 a neglected dam above Johnstown, Pennsylvania, gave way, and a wall of water tore through the town.
In 1900 a hurricane drove the sea over Galveston, Texas, the deadliest natural disaster in American history.
Two years later, on Martinique, Mount Pelee sent a cloud of burning gas over Saint-Pierre. Within minutes the city was gone.
In 1906 the San Andreas Fault slipped under San Francisco. The shaking and the fires that followed destroyed much of the city.
In 1908 something exploded in the sky over Siberia and flattened millions of trees, most likely a small asteroid or comet.
That same year, an earthquake and tsunami destroyed Messina and Reggio in southern Italy, killing about eighty thousand people.
In April 1912 the Titanic struck an iceberg on her maiden voyage and sank, with too few lifeboats. New rules for safety at sea followed.
In 1917, in the harbour of Halifax, a ship full of explosives collided with another and blew up, levelling the north of the city.
In 1923 the Great Kanto earthquake struck Tokyo and Yokohama at lunchtime, and fires from cooking stoves swept the wooden districts.
In the thirties, drought and bare soil raised giant dust storms over the American Plains, and many farm families fled west.
In 1931 the Yangtze, the Yellow and the Huai all flooded at once, and disease and famine deepened one of history's worst disasters.
In 1937 the airship Hindenburg burst into flames while landing in New Jersey. Caught on film, it ended the age of the great airships.
In the winter of 1952 a fog thick with coal smoke settled on London. Deaths surged, and Britain passed its first Clean Air Act.
From 1959, after the Great Leap Forward and failed harvests, famine spread across China, one of the deadliest in history.
In 1960 southern Chile felt the strongest earthquake ever measured, and its tsunamis crossed the Pacific to Hawaii and Japan.
On Good Friday in 1964, Alaska shook for minutes on end, and the quake helped prove the theory of plate tectonics.
In 1970 a cyclone drowned the low coast of what is now Bangladesh, and anger at the slow relief fed the push for independence.
In 1975 a typhoon burst the Banqiao dam and dozens more in China, a catastrophe kept secret for years.
In the early hours of a summer night in 1976, an earthquake levelled the Chinese industrial city of Tangshan.
In 1977, on a foggy runway in Tenerife, two jumbo jets collided, the deadliest accident in the history of flight.
In 1979 a reactor at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania partly melted down. Little radiation escaped, but trust in nuclear power fell.
In May 1980 Mount St. Helens blew out its north side, after the largest landslide in recorded history.
In 1984 poison gas leaked from a pesticide plant in Bhopal, India, into the homes around it, one of the worst industrial accidents ever.
In September 1985 an earthquake hit Mexico City, whose old lakebed made the shaking worse, and many buildings fell.
Two months later, a small eruption in Colombia melted ice into mudflows that buried the town of Armero in the night. The warnings came too late.
In January 1986 the shuttle Challenger broke apart just after launch, killing all seven aboard, a teacher among them.
That April a reactor exploded at Chernobyl. Radiation spread across Europe, and a wide zone around the plant is closed to this day.
In 1989 the tanker Exxon Valdez ran aground in Alaska and spilled crude oil into waters rich in wildlife.
In 1991 Mount Pinatubo erupted in the Philippines. Warnings saved thousands, and its sulphur cooled the planet for a year or two.
In January 1995 an earthquake struck Kobe in Japan, toppling buildings and an elevated highway, and killing more than six thousand.
In 1998 Hurricane Mitch stalled over Central America, and its floods and landslides killed about eleven thousand people.
In 2003 the shuttle Columbia broke up on its way home, its wing damaged at launch by a piece of foam.
On Boxing Day 2004 an undersea quake off Sumatra sent giant waves across the Indian Ocean, striking coasts from Indonesia to Sri Lanka.
In 2005 Hurricane Katrina broke the floodwalls of New Orleans, and much of the city went under water.
That October an earthquake in Kashmir killed some eighty thousand people.
In 2008 Cyclone Nargis struck Myanmar and killed around a hundred and forty thousand.
Days later an earthquake shook Sichuan in China, and the collapse of many schools raised hard questions about how they were built.
In January 2010 an earthquake struck close to Port-au-Prince, the capital of Haiti, and much of the city fell.
That spring the Deepwater Horizon rig exploded in the Gulf of Mexico, and oil gushed from the seabed for months.
In March 2011 the Fukushima nuclear plant in Japan lost its cooling, and several reactors melted down.
It began with the strongest quake ever recorded in Japan, off Tohoku, and a tsunami that swept whole towns away.
In 2013 the Rana Plaza factory near Dhaka collapsed on garment workers told to return despite the cracks in its walls.
Later that year Typhoon Haiyan killed more than six thousand people.
In 2014 Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 vanished with two hundred and thirty-nine people on board.
In 2015 an earthquake in Nepal killed nearly nine thousand, toppled old temples and set off an avalanche on Everest.
In 2017 Hurricane Maria devastated Puerto Rico and Dominica, leaving homes without power for months.
In 2019 fire destroyed the roof and spire of Notre-Dame in Paris. Five years later, the cathedral reopened.
In 2020 a store of ammonium nitrate, left for years in a warehouse, exploded at the port of Beirut and wrecked much of the city.
In February 2023 two huge earthquakes struck southern Turkey and Syria, killing tens of thousands.
That September Storm Daniel burst two dams above Derna in Libya, and thousands died in a single night.
In October 2024 torrential rain sent floods through the towns around Valencia, killing more than two hundred people.
In January 2025 wind-driven fires burned through Los Angeles, one of the costliest disasters in American history.
That March a great earthquake struck central Myanmar near Mandalay, felt as far away as Bangkok.
In June 2025 an Air India jet crashed into a medical college moments after taking off from Ahmedabad.
And in October 2025 Hurricane Melissa, one of the strongest ever seen in the Atlantic, struck Jamaica.
Each disaster left its grief, and its lessons for those who came after.
